::: {#exm-data-augmentation}

#### Noise and shifts for the digits

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Three 8 by 8 grayscale images of the same training digit:
#|   the original, a copy with random noise added to every pixel,
#|   and a copy moved one pixel to the right.


def add_noise(images, generator, sd=0.2):
    # Add independent normal noise with standard deviation `sd` to every pixel.
    return images + sd * torch.randn(images.shape, generator=generator)


def shift_images(images, rows, cols):
    # Move each 8-by-8 image by (rows, cols) pixels, filling the gap with 0.
    grid = images.reshape(-1, 8, 8)
    moved = torch.roll(grid, shifts=(rows, cols), dims=(1, 2))
    if rows > 0:
        moved[:, :rows, :] = 0
    if rows < 0:
        moved[:, rows:, :] = 0
    if cols > 0:
        moved[:, :, :cols] = 0
    if cols < 0:
        moved[:, :, cols:] = 0
    return moved.reshape(-1, 64)


example = x_train[:1]
noisy = add_noise(example, torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
shifted = shift_images(example, 0, 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6, 2.2), layout="constrained")
for ax, image, title in zip(axes, [example, noisy, shifted], ["original", "noise", "shifted"]):
    ax.imshow(image.reshape(8, 8), cmap="gray_r");
    ax.set_title(title);
    ax.axis("off");
plt.show()
```

The first training image is a `r py$y_train[0]$item()`.
Adding normal noise with standard deviation 0.2 to every pixel leaves it recognizable,
and so does moving it one pixel to the right.
Both are candidate transformations for [data augmentation](#def-data-augmentation) on the digits.

:::
